title: Chromatin accessibility classification of TAD boundaries discloses new architectural proteins.

verified.what_i_actually_checked: Unzipped the supplement and opened Jacome_Lopez_Supplemental_Tables.xlsx in pandas: Table S3 holds 4,173 boundary windows in four side-by-side blocks (Type I 2,047, II 498, III 542, IV 1,086), every window exactly 20,000 bp wide, 23 chromosomes, 0 duplicate coordinates. Pulled the 296 ENCODE ChIP-seq accessions out of Table S4, downloaded 4 of them (CTCF ENCFF002CEL, REST ENCFF895QLA, ZNF316 ENCFF788EBS, SMC3 ENCFF041YQC; all hg19 'optimal IDR thresholded peaks', ~0.5-1.5 MB each), intersected them with the boundaries and reproduced the paper's trend: CTCF occupies 69.6% of Type I boundaries falling monotonically to 53.1% of Type IV, with the same monotone drop for REST, ZNF316 and SMC3. Ran a leave-one-chromosome-out logistic regression on those 8 occupancy features for Type I vs Type IV (n=3,133): area under the ROC curve 0.634 (random forest 0.607, dummy 0.500). Listed both GEO series: processed Hi-C contact matrices per sample are 25-53 MB (first sequencing run) and 171-426 MB (second run), the series RAW tars are 2.5 GB and 1.3 GB.
verified.what_came_from_paper_text_only: That the four classes correspond to HindIII digestion times of 0.25, 1, 3 and 12 hours; that boundaries were called with the TAD-separation score in HiCExplorer v3.7.6 at 20-kb resolution with a false-discovery-rate cutoff of 0.00005 on replicate-merged matrices; that coordinates are hg19 (stated in Methods, not written anywhere in the spreadsheet, though my hg19 ENCODE intersections corroborate it); the ATAC-seq and quantitative-PCR validation of the accessibility ordering; the CRISPR deletion result. I did not download the Hi-C matrices or recompute any insulation score.

a1_downloadable.note: Supplementary workbook opened directly from the Europe PMC supplement zip, no login. ENCODE peak files and GEO matrices are public; I downloaded four ENCODE files successfully.

a2_label_is_a_column.note: The accessibility class (Type I-IV) is explicit in the file, but as four side-by-side column blocks rather than a label column; one reshape in pandas turns it into a tidy column. No inference across sources needed.

a3_inputs_present.note: Table S3 holds only genomic coordinates - no sequence, no features. Inputs must be fetched: either one hg19 reference genome (a single bulk download) or the 296 ENCODE accessions listed in Table S4 (~300 MB total). 296 bulk file downloads is not 'thousands of lookups'; I verified 4 of them download and intersect cleanly.

a4_units_stated.note: Coordinates are base pairs on hg19 (build stated in Methods only, not in the file - a real trap). Label is an ordered category tied to digestion times of 0.25/1/3/12 hours, stated in the paper.

a5_enough_rows.note: 4,173 labelled 20-kb windows counted in the file; 3,133 if restricted to the Type I vs Type IV contrast. Above the ~400-row classification floor.

a6_fits_laptop.working_set: ~0.4 GB of ENCODE peak files plus a 4,173-row table; a 3 GB genome FASTA only if DNA sequence features are used
a6_fits_laptop.note: Trivially laptop-scale. The 2.5 GB GEO RAW tar is not needed; individual 25-53 MB matrices are separately downloadable if insulation scores are ever recomputed.

a7_counts_match_paper.note: The per-class counts are not written in the paper text (Fig. 1C is a bar chart), so they cannot be cross-checked directly; but my CTCF occupancy by class (69.6% -> 53.1%) closely tracks the paper's reported 68% -> 46% at 5-kb resolution, which validates both coordinates and labels.

a8_label_provenance.note: The label is which digestion time a HiCExplorer TAD-separation-score call first appeared at - a deterministic caller run on physically measured Hi-C, not another machine-learning model's output, and not computable from any feature we would use. Two caveats: it is a thresholded call, and Table S2 shows valid-pair depth varies across time points (9.1-13.2 M at early times), so class membership partly encodes library depth.

B1.why: One sheet, but four side-by-side blocks; features live in 296 external ENCODE files. Seen in the file.

B2.why: xlsx parsed first try in pandas, but needs header skipping and a block reshape; not clean csv.

B3.why: All four classes from one cell line, one enzyme, one TAD caller - fully comparable. Verified in file.

B4.why: No censored cells, but the label is interval-censored by design: never-called boundaries are simply absent.

B5.why: Checked in the file: 0 duplicate chr/start/end across all 4,173 rows, no class overlap.

B6.why: Methods explain the classes; the sheet itself has no column headers, no README, no genome build.

C1.why: Framed as 'do published boundary-strength predictors recover this orthogonal accessibility ordering?', either answer informs.

C2.why: pTADS, preciseTAD, CT-TADB, Akita, Orca, C.Origami all open with cross-cell-line or held-out-chromosome evaluation.

C3.why: Only the digestion-time label is new; the protein-occupancy-predicts-strength finding is the paper's own result.

C4.why: Measuring boundary strength needs deep Hi-C plus a digestion time course - slow and costly. From paper Methods.

C5.why: I computed the dummy (AUC 0.500) and an occupancy baseline (0.634); pTADS and CT-TADB publish numbers.

D1.why: HyenaDNA and Nucleotide Transformer are open-weight DNA backbones matching 20-kb hg19 windows.

D2.why: 20-kb windows exceed most DNA model contexts; needs tiling and pooling, ~15 CPU hours of embedding (estimated).

D3.why: HyenaDNA is Apache-2.0 and DNABERT-2 permissive; no licence blocks this use.

E1.why: Leave-one-chromosome-out is the natural split; I actually ran it over the 23 chromosomes present.

E2.why: 23 chromosomes with 53-406 boundaries each, counted in the file.

E3.why: Computed: majority class 65.3% for Type I vs IV, dummy AUC 0.500.

E4.why: Two Hi-C replicates per time point in GEO, but calls were on merged matrices; re-calling needed.

E5.why: CTCF occupancy must fall from Type I to Type IV - I verified it does (69.6% to 53.1%).

E6.why: Label shuffling and per-protein ablation are one line each on a 4,173-row table.

E7.why: Rao et al. GSE63525 5-kb K562 boundaries, plus GM12878/HCT116 boundaries and 4D Nucleome Hi-C.

E8.why: I already approximately reproduced the paper's CTCF occupancy percentages; pTADS code is on GitHub.

G1.why: hg19 genomic coordinates in the file - a standard identifier for every 3D-genome and epigenome resource.

G2.why: 296 ENCODE K562 accessions already listed in Table S4; 4D Nucleome and AlphaGenome Atlas join on coordinates.

G3.why: Peaks-within-window is clean one-to-many; collapse rule is peak count or summed signal, which I used.

G4.why: Combination asks which protein modules beyond CTCF set strength - largely what the paper already did.

H1.why: Weak boundaries (Type IV, n=1,086) are present, but non-boundary regions are absent from the table.

H2.why: One cell line (K562), one lab, one enzyme (HindIII), one TAD caller. From paper and file.

H3.why: The honest claim writes cleanly in one sentence; see honest_claim_h3.

H4.why: Paper is explicit about 20-kb resolution limits and validates at 5 kb and by quantitative PCR.

I1.why: 3D-genome groups: Furlan-Magaril lab (UNAM), Fudenberg lab, the 4D Nucleome consortium.

I2.why: Would at best reorder a candidate list for CRISPR deletion tests; the paper already picked ZNF316/EMSY.

I3.why: A per-boundary class probability only loosely matches the real decision, 'which protein to delete next'.

I4.why: My 8-feature logistic reached only 0.634; a CTCF-count threshold may capture most of it.

J1.why: Real grouped splits, negative controls and an optional frozen DNA backbone - the ML skills wanted.

J2.why: 3D-genome biology is specialised, but the CTCF positive control gives a usable sanity check.

J3.why: A tidy hg19 BED of 4,173 classified boundaries plus a 296-protein occupancy matrix is shareable alone.

J4.why: No time budget set yet; the feature table is ~8 hours, so a 2-3 week box is plausible but unwritten.

J5.why: Kill condition is obvious (full 296-protein matrix fails to beat AUC 0.75) but not yet written down.

existing_models.name: pTADS (random forest for TAD boundary presence plus a lasso-based boundary strength score, Briefings in Bioinformatics 2021)
existing_models.score_and_split: Evaluated across seven cell lines and three TAD-calling methods; R code at github.com/chrom3DEpi/pTADS. Exact numbers not retrieved - I read the abstract and a search summary, not the full paper.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Not retrieved; the abstract emphasises cross-cell-line generalisability as the achievement rather than naming a gap.

existing_models.name: CT-TADB (hybrid convolutional-neural-network plus transformer predicting TAD boundaries from DNA sequence and histone marks, npj Systems Biology and Applications 2026)
existing_models.score_and_split: Area under the ROC curve 0.932-0.950, trained on six human cell lines, and reported to capture GM12878 vs K562 boundary gain/loss events. From the search summary and abstract, not from running it.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Cell-type transfer without Hi-C; the paper's selling point is avoiding Hi-C entirely.

existing_models.name: preciseTAD (transfer-learning framework for base-pair-resolution domain boundary prediction, Bioinformatics 2022)
existing_models.score_and_split: Distributed as a Bioconductor package; reported numbers not retrieved.

existing_models.name: Akita, Orca and C.Origami (deep networks predicting Hi-C contact maps, and hence insulation, from DNA sequence; Nature Methods 2020, Nature Genetics 2022, Nature Biotechnology 2023)
existing_models.score_and_split: C.Origami's paper benchmarks all four on insulation-score correlation and distance-stratified contact correlation on held-out chromosomes; weights and code are public for all three.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Cell-type-specific prediction without measured CTCF and accessibility tracks remains the stated frontier.

existing_models.name: Integrating heterogeneity into TAD boundary prediction (NAR Genomics and Bioinformatics 2026)
existing_models.score_and_split: Concluded that DNA sequence alone is insufficient for human TAD boundary prediction across a range of classical and deep architectures. From the search summary only.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Sequence-only prediction in human; multi-modal epigenetic input is needed.

backbone.name: HyenaDNA (long-context DNA language model, small checkpoints run on CPU); Nucleotide Transformer v2-50M as an alternative
backbone.hardware: CPU-only laptop; 20-kb windows tiled into 1-kb chunks and mean-pooled, embeddings cached once
backbone.licence: HyenaDNA Apache-2.0 (permissive); Nucleotide Transformer v2 is non-commercial, which is acceptable here

integration.partner_dataset: ENCODE K562 ChIP-seq (the 296 accessions already listed in the paper's Table S4, all hg19 optimal IDR thresholded peaks) plus Rao et al. GSE63525 Hi-C for 5-kb boundaries and other cell types
integration.join_key: hg19 genomic coordinates (overlap of a peak with a 20-kb boundary window)
integration.bigger_question_one_sentence: Which combinations of the 296 measured K562 proteins, beyond CTCF, distinguish a strongly insulating boundary from a weak one, and does that rule still hold in a different cell type?

controls.positive_control: CTCF occupancy and signal must rank Type I above Type IV - I verified this holds in the actual files (69.6% of Type I boundaries carry a CTCF peak versus 53.1% of Type IV), and any model that does not recover it is broken.
controls.negative_control: Shuffle the Type labels within chromosome and confirm the area under the ROC curve collapses to 0.50; ablate CTCF alone and see how much of the 0.634 baseline survives; swap in 4,173 random hg19 20-kb windows, which should be separable from boundaries but not ordered by type.
controls.external_validation: The 5-kb K562 boundaries derived from Rao et al. GSE63525, and GM12878/HCT116 boundaries (the paper's own cross-cell-type comparison), give a held-out-cell-type test; 4D Nucleome Hi-C is a second independent source.

honest_claim_h3: From protein occupancy and DNA sequence at a 20-kb window, we can predict - in K562 cells only, and only among windows that HiCExplorer called as a boundary at some digestion time - whether that boundary was detected at the earliest (most accessible) or only the latest (least accessible) digestion time, at roughly the accuracy an occupancy-only model already gives.

plain_idea.one_liner: Use protein binding and DNA sequence at a genome boundary to predict how strongly that boundary blocks contacts between neighbouring chromosome domains.
plain_idea.train_on: 4,173 windows of 20,000 base pairs each (counted in the file), each described by which of 296 proteins have a binding peak there in K562 leukaemia cells, and optionally by the DNA sequence itself.
plain_idea.predict: A four-level accessibility class (Type I most accessible to Type IV least). The true answer comes from Hi-C experiments in which chromatin was cut with the enzyme HindIII for 0.25, 1, 3 or 12 hours: a boundary that shows up after the shortest digestion is the most accessible.
plain_idea.why_worthwhile: Groups studying genome folding would get a ranked shortlist of proteins, beyond CTCF, that set how firmly a boundary insulates - the next CRISPR deletion to try. Even a failure tells us the digestion-time ordering is too noisy to model, which is worth knowing before anyone builds on it.

more_or_better_data.why: Smaller and narrower than the competition - 4,173 boundaries in one cell line versus pTADS's seven cell lines and CT-TADB's six. The only edge is the label type: a digestion-time accessibility ordering measured in the same Hi-C experiment, which no existing model was trained on.

confidence_score.why: Two Hi-C replicates per digestion time are deposited in GEO, so label reproducibility could be estimated - but the paper called boundaries on replicate-merged matrices, so per-boundary confidence would require re-calling from the 25-53 MB matrices. I did not check whether pTADS or CT-TADB report calibrated confidence.

models_beatable.why: CT-TADB (2026) reports area under the ROC curve of 0.932-0.950 with a convolutional-plus-transformer architecture evaluated across six cell lines, and Akita/Orca/C.Origami are benchmarked on held-out chromosomes with open weights. Only pTADS (2021, random forest) looks dated.

guaranteed_improvement.why: Fails on 'same quantity, same way': existing models predict boundary presence or Hi-C-derived insulation, whereas our label is which digestion time a call first appeared at. The evaluation split would also differ, since they train across cell lines and we have one.

label_elsewhere.sources: Boundary insulation strength is public for many cell types: Rao et al. GSE63525 (cited by this paper), ENCODE and 4D Nucleome Hi-C, and the 3D Genome Browser / TADKB boundary collections. Known resources, plus GSE63525 confirmed in the paper's Table S4. The specific digestion-time class, however, exists only in this paper.
label_elsewhere.join_key: Genomic coordinates plus genome build (hg19 here)
label_elsewhere.why: Insulation scores for tens of thousands of boundaries across many cell types give both extra training data and a ready external test of whether a strength model generalises past K562.

risks: Neighbouring 20-kb boundary windows on the same chromosome share local CTCF clusters and large-scale compartment context, so a random split would put near-duplicate regions in both train and test.

Sequencing depth differs across digestion time points (9.1-13.2 million valid pairs at early times per Table S2), and more reads means more boundary calls, so the class label partly encodes library depth rather than biology.

Chromatin accessibility is the basis of the label and is also what makes ChIP-seq peaks callable, so any protein's peak presence is partly a readout of accessibility itself - a soft circularity that inflates occupancy features.
The paper's own discovery process selected CTCF, REST, ZNF316 and EMSY from the same 296 datasets, so using those four as hand-picked features would be selecting on the test set.
leakage_plan.split: Leave-one-chromosome-out using the chr column, which I confirmed is present in Table S3 and holds 23 chromosomes with 53-406 boundaries each; I ran this split already. For external validation, hold out a whole cell type (GM12878 or HCT116 boundaries).
checks: Shuffle the Type labels within chromosome and confirm the area under the ROC curve returns to 0.50.
Train on CTCF peak count alone and see how much of the 0.634 occupancy baseline it explains - if nearly all, the other 295 proteins are decoration.
Regress class on a per-window read-depth proxy from the Hi-C matrices and check whether depth alone predicts the label.
Check nearest-neighbour genomic distance between each test boundary and its closest training boundary, and re-evaluate after excluding pairs within 1 Mb.
leakage_plan.verdict: Manageable: the chromosome split is easy and I have already run it, but the depth confound in the label and the accessibility-drives-peak-calling circularity are genuine and need the explicit checks above.

success_criteria.metric: Area under the ROC curve for Type I versus Type IV under leave-one-chromosome-out, because the decision a 3D-genome lab makes is a ranked shortlist of boundaries and proteins to test; plus Spearman correlation between predicted and measured ordinal class for the ranking use.
success_criteria.baselines: Measured by me on the real files: dummy 0.500, majority class 65.3%, logistic regression on CTCF/REST/ZNF316/SMC3 occupancy 0.634, random forest 0.607, all leave-one-chromosome-out. Published comparators are CT-TADB's 0.932-0.950 and pTADS's cross-cell-line numbers, but those are for a different label (boundary presence) and are not directly comparable.
success_criteria.success: Area under the ROC curve of at least 0.75 on held-out chromosomes for Type I versus Type IV using the full 296-protein occupancy matrix, with CTCF ablated performance still above 0.65 - i.e. the gain is not all CTCF.
success_criteria.kill: If the full 296-protein matrix does not beat 0.70 under leave-one-chromosome-out within one week, stop: the digestion-time label is too noisy to carry a model.

ambitious.why: Publishes 3D-genome method and benchmark papers; would need the model to identify and functionally validate a protein module that sets boundary strength beyond CTCF, across more than one cell type.

realistic.why: The likely result - published boundary-strength predictors partly recover an orthogonally measured accessibility ordering, with a modest held-out-chromosome number from one cell line - is exactly the scope of its short method and evaluation papers.

fallback.journal: Bioinformatics (Application Note) or a bioRxiv preprint
fallback.why: Even a negative result plus a tidy, documented release of 4,173 accessibility-classified hg19 boundaries joined to a 296-protein occupancy matrix is a usable community resource.

pitch.headline: 4,173 genome boundaries labelled by how fast an enzyme cuts them - an accessibility ordering no existing boundary predictor was trained on.
pitch.what_makes_the_data_unusual: The strength label comes from the same Hi-C experiment as the boundary calls, via a 0.25/1/3/12-hour digestion time course, so accessibility and insulation are measured together rather than joined across assays.
pitch.the_win: Push leave-one-chromosome-out area under the ROC curve for most- versus least-accessible boundaries from the 0.634 I measured with four proteins to above 0.75 with all 296, and name which proteins carry the gain once CTCF is ablated.
pitch.even_if_it_fails: We learn the digestion-time class is too noisy or too depth-confounded to model, which directly bounds how much weight the paper's accessibility hierarchy can bear.
pitch.who_wants_it: The Furlan-Magaril lab (UNAM) and sequence-to-contact-map groups such as Fudenberg's; it would reorder which candidate architectural protein gets the next CRISPR deletion.

ml_idea: Build a tidy hg19 table of the 4,173 accessibility-classified boundaries joined to binary and signal-weighted occupancy for all 296 ENCODE K562 ChIP-seq datasets listed in Table S4, then predict the Type I-IV class under leave-one-chromosome-out. Two arms: (1) occupancy-only gradient boosting, with CTCF ablation to test whether anything beyond CTCF carries signal; (2) a frozen HyenaDNA embedding of the 20-kb sequence with a linear head, to ask whether sequence alone adds anything over occupancy. The headline experiment is a re-evaluation: score published predictors (pTADS, preciseTAD, and Akita/Orca insulation predictions) against this independently measured accessibility ordering and report whether they recover it.

effort.compute_note: Timed directly: unzipping and parsing Table S3, downloading 4 ENCODE peak files and intersecting them took under three minutes, and the leave-one-chromosome-out logistic regression and random forest ran in seconds on 3,133 rows. The 8-hour and 5-minute figures scale that to 296 files and 296 features; the 15 embedding hours is an unverified estimate for tiling 83 megabases of sequence through a small DNA language model on CPU.
effort.cheapest_killing_check: Already done: leave-one-chromosome-out area under the ROC curve for Type I versus Type IV using CTCF, REST, ZNF316 and SMC3 occupancy is only 0.634. The next and decisive check is whether the full 296-protein matrix clears 0.75; if not, stop.

verdict_reason: Every Part A killer passes and I verified it in the files: 4,173 clean 20-kb hg19 windows, four explicit accessibility classes, zero duplicates, and the paper's CTCF trend reproduced in my own intersections (69.6% of Type I versus 53.1% of Type IV). But the field is saturated with open, honestly evaluated models - pTADS predicts boundary strength, CT-TADB (2026) reports 0.932-0.950 across six cell lines, and Akita/Orca/C.Origami are benchmarked on held-out chromosomes - so C2 scores 0. The data is one cell line, one lab, one enzyme and one TAD caller, the label is a thresholded algorithmic call partly confounded by sequencing depth, and my own leave-one-chromosome-out baseline reached only 0.634, so the likely outcome is a modest number in a crowded area. Keep it as a cheap, publishable re-evaluation project - do published boundary-strength predictors recover this orthogonal accessibility ordering? - rather than a priority.
